8A

Key ideas

Momentum

Definitions

Momentum, p: the product of an object’s mass and velocity
Mass: a body’s resistance to acceleration when a force is applied
Inertia: a body’s tendency to resist a change in its state of motion
Closed system: a system that does not allow the transfer of mass or energy to the surrounding environment
Law of conservation of momentum: for a collision involving two or more objects in a closed system, the total momentum will remain the same

Formulas

Formula 8A–1 Momentum
p=mvp = mvp=mv

Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, 8A glossary and formula boxes3
8A

Key ideas

Momentum

Definitions

Kinetic energy: the energy due to movement. It is measured in joules (J) and is a scalar
Elastic collision: a collision in which the total kinetic energy is the same both before and after the collision
Inelastic collision: a collision in which the total kinetic energy is larger before the collision than after the collision. The ‘missing’ energy is often converted into other forms, such as thermal energy and sound energy
Impulse: the change in momentum of an object, caused by a force acting for a certain amount of time

Formulas

Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, 8A glossary and formula boxes4
8A

New knowledgeModelling motion with momentum

Momentum

A heavy object is harder to stop than a lighter object at the same speed.

This simple fact helps you to develop an understanding of momentum.

Momentum, ppp, is an object’s mass multiplied by its velocity. [Formula 8A–1] Momentum is a vector quantity and it must have both magnitude and direction.

The direction of the momentum vector and velocity vector will always be the same.

Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 8, p. 75
8A

New knowledgeModelling motion with momentum

Momentum

Momentum can only be changed when a net external force is applied.

Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 8, p. 76
8A

New knowledgeMomentum and inertia

Momentum

It is important to note that momentum and inertia are two different concepts.

An object that is stationary has no momentum, but it has inertia.

Inertia is linked to Newton’s first law of motion and is defined as a body’s tendency to resist a change in its state of motion when acted upon by a net force.

The amount of inertia an object has depends only on the amount of mass that it has – the greater the mass, the greater the inertia.

Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 8, p. 77
8A

New knowledgeMomentum and inertia

Momentum

The law of conservation of momentum states that for a collision involving two or more objects in a closed system, the total momentum will remain the same.

That is, the total momentum of a system will remain constant as long as no external net force acts on the system.

The law of conservation of momentum can be expressed mathematically as shown in the Formula 8A–2 box. [Formula 8A–2] For one-dimensional collisions it is important to use a positive or a negative sign to indicate the direction of straight-line motion.

Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 8, p. 78
8A

New knowledgeTwo objects colliding and combining

Momentum

In some cases, two or more objects may collide and then combine and move as one.

The resulting object will have the mass of: m1u1+m2u2+…=m3v3m_1u_1 + m_2u_2 + \ldots = m_3v_3m1​u1​+m2​u2​+…=m3​v3​

Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 8, p. 99
8A

New knowledgeA single object breaking apart

Momentum

In other cases, a single object may break apart into two or more other objects in what is known as an explosive collision.

In this case, the law of conservation of momentum still applies: m1u1=m2v2+m3v3+…m_1u_1 = m_2v_2 + m_3v_3 + \ldotsm1​u1​=m2​v2​+m3​v3​+…

Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 8, p. 910

Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 8, p. 1111
8A

New knowledgeElastic and inelastic collisions

Momentum

Collisions may be elastic or inelastic.

If they are elastic, then it is possible to predict the final velocity of the two colliding objects.

Completely elastic collisions occur between gas particles and the walls of the container.

However, most collisions are not elastic and some of the energy is converted into thermal energy and sound energy.

Figure 8A–3 Pool balls moving towards each other before the collision
Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 8, p. 1112
8A

New knowledgeElastic and inelastic collisions

Momentum

If a collision is 100% inelastic, then all of the energy is converted into thermal energy and sound energy and the two colliding objects will be stationary after the collision.

To determine if a collision is elastic or inelastic, the total kinetic energy must be calculated before and after the collision.

If the total kinetic energy before and after the collision is equal, then it is an elastic collision.

If the total kinetic energy before the collision is greater than the total kinetic energy after the collision, then it is an inelastic collision.

Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 8, p. 1113
8A

New knowledgeChange in momentum (impulse)

Momentum

When all objects are considered in a collision, momentum is conserved provided that no net external force acts on the system.

However, if only one object is considered, then momentum may not be conserved (as the momentum is transferred to other objects that are not considered).

When the velocity of an object changes, its momentum also changes.

An increase in velocity means an increase in momentum, and a decrease in velocity means a decrease in momentum.

Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 8, p. 1214
8A

New knowledgeChange in momentum (impulse)

Momentum

This change in momentum is sometimes referred to as impulse. [Formula 8A–4] Remember that the only way to change an object’s velocity (and therefore its momentum) is to apply a net force on the object.

The change in momentum (the impulse) is a vector quantity; it requires both a magnitude and a direction.

Momentum has a relationship with average net force on the object, as the change in momentum over time is the average net force on the object (this is because it takes a net external force to change momentum).

This can be seen in the following way.

Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 8, p. 1215

New knowledgeChange in momentum (impulse)

Momentum

Start with Newton’s second law for an average net force: Fav=maavF_{\text{av}} = ma_{\text{av}}Fav​=maav​ Note that an average acceleration is equivalent to a change in velocity over time: Fav=mΔvΔtF_{\text{av}} = \frac{m\Delta v}{\Delta t}Fav​=ΔtmΔv​ Using the definition of momentum, recognise that the numerator is a change in momentum: Fav=ΔpΔtF_{\text{av}} = \frac{\Delta p}{\Delta t}Fav​=ΔtΔp​ Finally, rearrange this equation, using the definition of impulse: Δp=FavΔt=I=mv−mu\Delta p = F_{\text{av}}\Delta t = I = mv - muΔp=Fav​Δt=I=mv−mu

Calculate the momentum of a 1.45×1031.45\times10^{3}1.45×103 kg car driving north at 72.0 km h−1^{-1}−1.
Key idea · Formula 8A–1 Momentump=mvp = mvp=mv

Working

Convert the speed from km h−1^{-1}−1 to m s−1^{-1}−1:
u=723.6=20.0 m s−1u = \frac{72}{3.6} = 20.0\text{ m s}^{-1}u=3.672​=20.0 m s−1
Substitute into the momentum equation:
p=mv=(1.45×103)(20)=2.9×104 kg m s−1p = mv = (1.45\times10^{3})(20) = 2.9\times10^{4}\text{ kg m s}^{-1}p=mv=(1.45×103)(20)=2.9×104 kg m s−1
Therefore, the momentum of the car is 2.9×1042.9\times10^{4}2.9×104 kg m s−1^{-1}−1 north.

We doMomentum in a head on collision

Momentum
A car of mass 1400 kg is moving to the right at a velocity of 20.0 m s−1^{-1}−1. It collides with a car of mass 1000 kg moving at 30.0 m s−1^{-1}−1 to the left. After the collision, the 1400 kg mass car moves to the left with a velocity of 12.5 m s−1^{-1}−1. Calculate the velocity of the 1000 kg car after the collision.
Key idea · Formula 8A–1 Momentump=mvp = mvp=mv

Working

Let moving to the right be the positive direction.
Before the collision: u1=20 m s−1u_1 = 20\text{ m s}^{-1}u1​=20 m s−1, u2=−30 m s−1u_2 = -30\text{ m s}^{-1}u2​=−30 m s−1, m1=1400m_1 = 1400m1​=1400 kg, m2=1000m_2 = 1000m2​=1000 kg
After the collision: v1=−12.5 m s−1v_1 = -12.5\text{ m s}^{-1}v1​=−12.5 m s−1
Rearrange the conservation of momentum formula to find v2v_2v2​:
m1u1+m2u2=m1v1+m2v2m_1u_1 + m_2u_2 = m_1v_1 + m_2v_2m1​u1​+m2​u2​=m1​v1​+m2​v2​
m2v2=m1u1+m2u2−m1v1m_2v_2 = m_1u_1 + m_2u_2 - m_1v_1m2​v2​=m1​u1​+m2​u2​−m1​v1​
v2=m1u1+m2u2−m1v1m2=(1400)(20)+(1000)(−30)−(1400)(−12.5)1000=15.5 m s−1v_2 = \frac{m_1u_1 + m_2u_2 - m_1v_1}{m_2} = \frac{(1400)(20) + (1000)(-30) - (1400)(-12.5)}{1000} = 15.5\text{ m s}^{-1}v2​=m2​m1​u1​+m2​u2​−m1​v1​​=1000(1400)(20)+(1000)(−30)−(1400)(−12.5)​=15.5 m s−1
Therefore, the 1000 kg car will be moving to the right at 15.5 m s−1^{-1}−1 after the collision.
15.5 m s−1^{-1}−1 to the right

Momentum
A car that has a mass of 1350 kg is moving in traffic at 13.9 m s−1^{-1}−1 north. The driver of the car is texting and rear ends a 1550 kg car in front of it that was moving at a velocity of 2.00 m s−1^{-1}−1 north when it was hit. The two cars stick and move as one. Calculate the velocity that the two cars will have after the collision.
Key idea · Formula 8A–1 Momentump=mvp = mvp=mv

Working

Let moving to the right be the positive direction.
Before the collision: u1=13.9 m s−1u_1 = 13.9\text{ m s}^{-1}u1​=13.9 m s−1, m1=1350m_1 = 1350m1​=1350 kg, u2=2.00 m s−1u_2 = 2.00\text{ m s}^{-1}u2​=2.00 m s−1, m2=1550m_2 = 1550m2​=1550 kg
After the collision:
m3=m1+m2=(1350)+(1550)=2900m_3 = m_1 + m_2 = (1350) + (1550) = 2900m3​=m1​+m2​=(1350)+(1550)=2900 kg
Rearrange the conservation of momentum formula to find v3v_3v3​:
m1u1+m2u2=m3v3m_1u_1 + m_2u_2 = m_3v_3m1​u1​+m2​u2​=m3​v3​
v3=m1u1+m2u2m3=(1350)(13.9)+(1550)(2.00)(2900)=7.54 m s−1v_3 = \frac{m_1u_1 + m_2u_2}{m_3} = \frac{(1350)(13.9) + (1550)(2.00)}{(2900)} = 7.54\text{ m s}^{-1}v3​=m3​m1​u1​+m2​u2​​=(2900)(1350)(13.9)+(1550)(2.00)​=7.54 m s−1
Therefore, the two cars will be moving to the right at 7.54 m s−1^{-1}−1 after the collision.

A person of mass 70.0 kg is skating on a frozen lake holding a 200 g ball. The person stops and then throws the ball south with a velocity of 21.3 m s−1^{-1}−1. Calculate the velocity of the person once the ball is thrown. Assume that the friction between the skater and the ice is negligible.
Key idea · Formula 8A–1 Momentump=mvp = mvp=mv

Working

Let south be the positive direction.
Before the collision: m1=m2+m3=0.2+70.0=70.2m_1 = m_2 + m_3 = 0.2 + 70.0 = 70.2m1​=m2​+m3​=0.2+70.0=70.2 kg, u1=0 m s−1u_1 = 0\text{ m s}^{-1}u1​=0 m s−1
After the collision: m2=0.200m_2 = 0.200m2​=0.200 kg, v2=21.3 m s−1v_2 = 21.3\text{ m s}^{-1}v2​=21.3 m s−1, m3=70.0m_3 = 70.0m3​=70.0 kg
Rearrange the conservation of momentum formula to find v3v_3v3​:
m1u1=m2v2+m3v3m_1u_1 = m_2v_2 + m_3v_3m1​u1​=m2​v2​+m3​v3​
m3v3=m1u1−m2v2m_3v_3 = m_1u_1 - m_2v_2m3​v3​=m1​u1​−m2​v2​
v3=m1u1−m2v2m3=(70.2)(0)−(0.200)(21.3)70.0=−0.0609 m s−1v_3 = \frac{m_1u_1 - m_2v_2}{m_3} = \frac{(70.2)(0) - (0.200)(21.3)}{70.0} = -0.0609\text{ m s}^{-1}v3​=m3​m1​u1​−m2​v2​​=70.0(70.2)(0)−(0.200)(21.3)​=−0.0609 m s−1
Therefore, the person will be moving north at 0.0609 m s−1^{-1}−1 after the ball is thrown.
0.0609 m s−1^{-1}−1 north

8A

We doInelastic collision

Momentum
Two billiard or pool balls, each with a mass of 0.160 kg, and moving with a constant speed of 5 m s−1^{-1}−1 collide head on with each other. After the collision, the balls separate, each moving with a speed of 4 m s−1^{-1}−1. A diagram of this situation is shown in Figure 8A–3 and 8A–4. a Show that the momentum of the balls is conserved. b Show that this collision is inelastic.
Key idea · Formula 8A–1 Momentump=mvp = mvp=mv

Working

a Calculate the total momentum just before and just after the collision:
∑pbefore=m1u1+m2u2=(0.160)(5)+(0.160)(−5)=0 kg m s−1\sum p_{\text{before}} = m_1u_1 + m_2u_2 = (0.160)(5) + (0.160)(-5) = 0\text{ kg m s}^{-1}∑pbefore​=m1​u1​+m2​u2​=(0.160)(5)+(0.160)(−5)=0 kg m s−1
∑pafter=m1v1+m2v2=(0.160)(4)+(0.160)(−4)=0 kg m s−1\sum p_{\text{after}} = m_1v_1 + m_2v_2 = (0.160)(4) + (0.160)(-4) = 0\text{ kg m s}^{-1}∑pafter​=m1​v1​+m2​v2​=(0.160)(4)+(0.160)(−4)=0 kg m s−1
Note that the velocity of one of the balls must be negative because the balls are travelling in opposite directions.
Since ∑pbefore=∑pafter\sum p_{\text{before}} = \sum p_{\text{after}}∑pbefore​=∑pafter​, momentum is conserved.
b Calculate the total kinetic energy before and after the collision:
∑Ek before=12m1(u1)2+12m2(u2)2=12(0.160)(5)2+12(0.160)(5)2=4 J\sum E_{\text{k before}} = \frac{1}{2}m_1(u_1)^2 + \frac{1}{2}m_2(u_2)^2 = \frac{1}{2}(0.160)(5)^2 + \frac{1}{2}(0.160)(5)^2 = 4\text{ J}∑Ek before​=21​m1​(u1​)2+21​m2​(u2​)2=21​(0.160)(5)2+21​(0.160)(5)2=4 J
∑Ek after=12m1(v1)2+12m2(v2)2=12(0.160)(4)2+12(0.160)(4)2=2.56 J\sum E_{\text{k after}} = \frac{1}{2}m_1(v_1)^2 + \frac{1}{2}m_2(v_2)^2 = \frac{1}{2}(0.160)(4)^2 + \frac{1}{2}(0.160)(4)^2 = 2.56\text{ J}∑Ek after​=21​m1​(v1​)2+21​m2​(v2​)2=21​(0.160)(4)2+21​(0.160)(4)2=2.56 J
Therefore, since ∑Ek before>∑Ek after\sum E_{\text{k before}} > \sum E_{\text{k after}}∑Ek before​>∑Ek after​, the collision is inelastic.
a 0 kg m s−1^{-1}−1 before and after; b 4 J > 2.56 J, inelastic
Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 8, p. 11, Worked example 8A-528

We doApplying impulse

Momentum
A person is travelling south in a car at 72 km h−1^{-1}−1 when they see an object on the road. They slam on the brakes and come to a complete stop in 4 seconds. The mass of the driver is 70 kg and the mass of the car is 1330 kg. a Calculate the change in momentum of the car and driver. b Calculate the average force that the road applies to the car in order to stop it.
Key idea · Formula 8A–1 Momentump=mvp = mvp=mv

Working

a Let south be the positive direction.
Convert the initial speed from km h−1^{-1}−1 to m s−1^{-1}−1: u=723.6=20 m s−1u = \frac{72}{3.6} = 20\text{ m s}^{-1}u=3.672​=20 m s−1
Find the change in momentum, noting that the final velocity is zero:
Δp=mv−mu=(70+1330)(0)−(70+1330)(20)=−2.8×104 kg m s−1\Delta p = mv - mu = (70 + 1330)(0) - (70 + 1330)(20) = -2.8\times10^{4}\text{ kg m s}^{-1}Δp=mv−mu=(70+1330)(0)−(70+1330)(20)=−2.8×104 kg m s−1
Therefore, the change in momentum (impulse) is 2.8×1042.8\times10^{4}2.8×104 kg m s−1^{-1}−1 north.
b Use the definition of impulse:
I=Δp=FavΔtI = \Delta p = F_{\text{av}}\Delta tI=Δp=Fav​Δt
Fav=ΔpΔt=2.8×1044=7000 NF_{\text{av}} = \frac{\Delta p}{\Delta t} = \frac{2.8\times10^{4}}{4} = 7000\text{ N}Fav​=ΔtΔp​=42.8×104​=7000 N
Therefore, the average force applied by the road is 7000 N north.
a 2.8×1042.8\times10^{4}2.8×104 kg m s−1^{-1}−1 north; b 7000 N north

You trySection 8A questions Q7

Momentum
A student sets up an experiment to test the effectiveness of crumple zones. The student places a crash cart with a digital force sensor at the top of a ramp. The cart is placed at the same height each time and the mass of the cart is the same each time. A heavy block is placed at the bottom of the ramp for the cart to collide into. A diagram of the student's set-up is shown below. The student takes a control run with no crumple zone and the digital force sensor graphs the force–time graph of the collision in red in the graph below. The student then makes their own prediction about the likely shape of the graph when a crumple zone is added to the cart. The student's prediction is shown in blue. Discuss the accuracy of the student's prediction. If you think the prediction is wrong, explain why and propose a correct prediction.

Working

The prediction is incorrect. The car has the same mass and it will have the same velocity when it reaches the block because it is being released from the same height each time. This means the momentum will be the same when the cart hits the block and therefore the change in momentum will be the same. The change in momentum (impulse) is given by the area under the force–time graph and the area under the red and blue graphs are not the same. A more correct prediction would be to have the same area under the graph, but the cart with the crumple zone would have a longer collision, which reduces the average forces.

u=273.6=7.5 m s−1u = \frac{27}{3.6} = 7.5\text{ m s}^{-1}u=3.627​=7.5 m s−1; v=633.6=17.5 m s−1v = \frac{63}{3.6} = 17.5\text{ m s}^{-1}v=3.663​=17.5 m s−1; Δp=mv−mu=(1300)(17.5)−(1300)(7.5)=1.30×104 kg m s−1\Delta p = mv - mu = (1300)(17.5) - (1300)(7.5) = 1.30\times10^{4}\text{ kg m s}^{-1}Δp=mv−mu=(1300)(17.5)−(1300)(7.5)=1.30×104 kg m s−1
Check-in set 2 · Q2 · 8A
A group of engineers are working together to design a new material for a diving board that will launch a diver to the greatest height. They test two the materials by building two prototype diving boards and measure the force applied to the material over time as a 70 kg person dives on the boards. Their results are shown below. a Calculate the impulse given to the person while in contact with the diving board. b Which material, A or B, should the engineers choose? Justify your answer.
a Area under the curve =(2)(0.5)(2800)(0.1)=280 kg m s−1= (2)(0.5)(2800)(0.1) = 280\text{ kg m s}^{-1}=(2)(0.5)(2800)(0.1)=280 kg m s−1. Or by: Area under the curve =(2)(0.5)(1400)(0.2)=280 kg m s−1= (2)(0.5)(1400)(0.2) = 280\text{ kg m s}^{-1}=(2)(0.5)(1400)(0.2)=280 kg m s−1. b Material B. In both cases the diver will reach the same vertical height as the impulse is the same. Material B has a greater time with which this impulse is given to the diver so, according to the formula F=IΔtF = \frac{I}{\Delta t}F=ΔtI​, the force on the diver will be reduced. This may reduce injury to the diver.
